'''''Adiantum hispidulum''''', commonly known as '''rough maidenhair fern''' or '''five-fingered jack''',  is a small [[fern]] in the family [[Pteridaceae]] of widespread distribution. It is found in [[Africa]], [[Australia]], [[Polynesia]], [[Malesia]], [[New Zealand]] and other Pacific Islands.<ref name=foa>{{cite web|title=''Adiantum hispidulum''|work=Flora of Australia Online|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/abrs/online-resources/flora/stddisplay.xsql?pnid=4557|access-date=2010-07-14|archive-date=2013-11-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131103214656/http://www.anbg.gov.au/abrs/online-resources/flora/stddisplay.xsql?pnid=4557|url-status=dead}}</ref>  Its fronds rise in clumps from rhizomes among rocks or in the soil in sheltered areas.

==Taxonomy==
''Adiantum hispidulum'' was first described by Swedish botanist [[Olof Swartz]] in 1802.<ref>{{APNI | name = ''Adiantum hispidulum'' Sw.  | id = 22233}}</ref> Its species name is derived from the [[Latin]] ''hispis'' "hair" and means "minutely hairy".<ref name=enc>{{cite book | last1=Elliot | first1=Rodger W. | last2=Jones | first2=David L. | last3=Blake | first3=Trevor |title=Encyclopaedia of Australian Plants Suitable for Cultivation: Vol. 2|year=1985|page=159 |publisher=Lothian Press |location=Port Melbourne |isbn=0-85091-143-5}}</ref> Five-fingered jack is an alternative vernacular name.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.noosanativeplants.com.au/plants/575/adiantum-hispidulum|title=''Adiantum hispidulum''|work=Welcome to Noosa's Native Plants|author=Stephanie Haslam|year=2007|access-date=19 July 2010|archive-date=3 April 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110403202940/http://www.noosanativeplants.com.au/plants/575/adiantum-hispidulum|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Description==
''Adiantum hispidulum'' grows in tufts or clumps among rocks or from the ground, its fronds arising from the short dark clumped rhizomes. The dark stalk measures up to {{convert|45|cm}} in length. The fronds are divided into long and short narrow triangular or elliptic pinnae (leafy branches), each of which is divided again into smaller roughly rectangular, diamond-, or fan-shaped pinnules. Each pinnule may have 1 to 20 spore clusters along its margins underneath. Young growth may have a pinkish tinge before it matures into the dark green foliage.<ref name=foa/><ref name=Fairley>{{cite book |author = Fairley A, Moore P |title=Native Plants of the Sydney District:An Identification Guide |year=2000 |edition= 2nd|publisher=Kangaroo Press |page=37|location=Kenthurst, NSW |isbn=0-7318-1031-7}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
The species ranges from tropical [[Eastern Africa]], including South Africa, Mozambique, Malawi, Kenya and Tanzania, as well as Madagascar and the Comoros, Mauritius, to Asia through [[Malesia]] to all states of Australia (with the exception of Tasmania<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.utas.edu.au/dicotkey/dicotkey/ferns/gAdiantum.htm|title=Key to Tasmanian Dicots}}</ref>), as well as New Zealand and Pacific islands.<ref>{{cite web |title=Entry for ADIANTUM hispidulum var. hispidulum [family ADIANTACEAE], Flora of Tropical East Africa | page=1 |url=http://plants.jstor.org/flora/ftea005971?cookieSet=1|work=JSTOR Plant Science|year=2002|author=Verdcourt, Bernard|access-date=19 July 2010}}</ref> A common plant, ''Adiantum hispidulum'' is often seen growing in moist areas. In Australia it is found near rocks, in rainforest or open forest.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Adiantum hispidulum''|work= PlantNET - NSW Flora Online|url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Adiantum~hispidulum|access-date=2010-07-14}}</ref>

Apart from its native range, it has naturalized in [[Macaronesia]] (the [[Azores]], [[Madeira]] and [[Canary Islands]]), the [[Southeastern United States]] and [[Hawaii]].<ref>{{cite web |title=World Plants: Complete Plant List |url=https://www.worldplants.de/world-plants-complete-list/complete-plant-list/?name=Adiantum-hispidulum#g- |website=www.worldplants.de |access-date=19 February 2022}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
''Adiantum hispidulum'' is grown as an [[ornamental plant]] that adapts readily to cultivation, although may be slow growing. It is more tolerant of sun and drying out than other fern species.<ref name=enc/> According to the [[Royal Horticultural Society]] Adiantum hispidulum is hardy down to {{convert|−5|to|−10|C}}.{{citation needed|date=February 2022}}
